params.text:
AN ICE CUBE MELTING

Ice is water whose molecules have stopped tumbling past each other
and locked into a pattern. Every molecule holds on to four
neighbours, and together they make a honeycomb of six-sided rings.
Melting is that pattern breaking up.

Here you build a tiny ice cube -- 768 water molecules, 3 nanometres
across; ten million of them side by side would make one cube for a
drink -- let it float in empty space, and see what heat does to it.
Twice: once at room temperature, once colder than any freezer.

Press Run. Everything takes a few minutes; read the notes while it
works.

1. BUILD THE CUBE

'Ice crystal' puts every molecule where ice puts it. Each oxygen
(red) points its two hydrogens (white) at two of its four
neighbours. Those hydrogen bonds are what hold ice together.

The water model is TIP4P/Ice: a water molecule drawn as four points
-- an oxygen, two hydrogens, and one invisible point that carries the
negative charge. Its numbers were chosen so that its ice melts at
the right temperature: 272 K, where real ice melts at 273 K,
0 degrees C.

'Define box' puts the cube in the middle of a 5.5 nm box of empty
space. Simulation boxes repeat in every direction, so the box has to
be big enough that the cube never feels the copy of itself next door.

params.raw:
; Minimisation: let every molecule settle into place.
;
; A crystal built from a recipe is never quite right -- a hydrogen a little
; too close to a neighbour here, a molecule a little twisted there. This walks
; every molecule downhill in energy until nothing is pushing hard any more.
; No time passes, and nothing moves afterwards: the cube is standing
; perfectly still, which is what 0 K, absolute zero, means.
integrator      = steep
emtol           = 100       ; stop when no force is bigger than this
nsteps          = 5000      ; or after this many tries

cutoff-scheme   = Verlet
coulombtype     = PME       ; every charge feels every other charge
rcoulomb        = 1.0       ; nm
vdwtype         = cut-off   ; molecules further apart than rvdw ignore each other's size
rvdw            = 1.0       ; nm
pbc             = xyz       ; the box repeats in every direction

params.text:
2. WARM: 300 K, 27 DEGREES C

Every molecule is given a speed that matches 300 K, and a thermostat
keeps it there. Then 100 picoseconds pass: 50,000 steps of 2
femtoseconds each. A femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a
second.

What happens: the corners go first, then the edges, then the faces
-- melting starts at the surface. Within about 30 ps the honeycomb
is gone, and the liquid pulls itself into a round drop. Why round:
surface tension. A ball is the shape with the least surface.

grompp warns once about stopping the cube from spinning. That is
expected, and allowed: see the last lines of the run settings.

params.raw:
; The ice cube at 300 K, which is 27 degrees C: room temperature.
;
; To try another temperature, change ref_t and gen_temp below -- both of
; them, to the same number -- and press Run again.
integrator           = md
dt                   = 0.002     ; one step is 2 femtoseconds (0.002 ps)
nsteps               = 50000     ; 50,000 steps: 100 picoseconds

nstxout-compressed   = 250       ; save a picture every 250 steps (0.5 ps)
nstenergy            = 500       ; and the energies, every 1 ps
nstlog               = 5000

cutoff-scheme        = Verlet
coulombtype          = PME
rcoulomb             = 1.0
vdwtype              = cut-off
rvdw                 = 1.0
pbc                  = xyz

; The thermostat: it keeps the temperature at ref_t, by speeding the
; molecules up or slowing them down a little at every step.
tcoupl               = v-rescale
tc-grps              = System
tau_t                = 0.1       ; how quickly it corrects, in ps
ref_t                = 300

; Give every molecule a speed to start with, picked at random the way
; speeds are spread at this temperature.
gen_vel              = yes
gen_temp             = 300
gen_seed             = 2026

; No pressure control: around the cube there is nothing but empty space.
pcoupl               = no

; Keep the cube in the middle of the picture: take away any drift and any
; spin it picks up. Safe only for a single lump that never touches the edge
; of the box -- which is what this is, and why grompp warns about it and is
; allowed one warning.
comm-mode            = angular

params.measure: Radius of gyration: how spread out it is (gyrate)

params.text:
3. COLD: 200 K, MINUS 73 DEGREES C

The same cube and the same settings, except the temperature. 200 K
is colder than any freezer: about as cold as the coldest nights in
Antarctica. The molecules shiver in place, but the honeycomb holds.

The outermost layer does loosen a little. The surface of ice is
slightly wet even well below freezing, which is part of why ice is
slippery.

Try it: set ref_t and gen_temp in the cold run's settings to 250
(minus 23 degrees C) and run it again. Tiny crystals melt at lower
temperatures than big ones, so this cube starts to melt even there
-- slowly.

params.raw:
; The ice cube at 200 K, which is -73 degrees C: colder than any freezer.
;
; To try another temperature, change ref_t and gen_temp below -- both of
; them, to the same number -- and press Run again.
integrator           = md
dt                   = 0.002     ; one step is 2 femtoseconds (0.002 ps)
nsteps               = 50000     ; 50,000 steps: 100 picoseconds

nstxout-compressed   = 250       ; save a picture every 250 steps (0.5 ps)
nstenergy            = 500       ; and the energies, every 1 ps
nstlog               = 5000

cutoff-scheme        = Verlet
coulombtype          = PME
rcoulomb             = 1.0
vdwtype              = cut-off
rvdw                 = 1.0
pbc                  = xyz

; The thermostat: it keeps the temperature at ref_t, by speeding the
; molecules up or slowing them down a little at every step.
tcoupl               = v-rescale
tc-grps              = System
tau_t                = 0.1       ; how quickly it corrects, in ps
ref_t                = 200

; Give every molecule a speed to start with, picked at random the way
; speeds are spread at this temperature.
gen_vel              = yes
gen_temp             = 200
gen_seed             = 2026

; No pressure control: around the cube there is nothing but empty space.
pcoupl               = no

; Keep the cube in the middle of the picture: take away any drift and any
; spin it picks up. Safe only for a single lump that never touches the edge
; of the box -- which is what this is, and why grompp warns about it and is
; allowed one warning.
comm-mode            = angular

params.measure: Radius of gyration: how spread out it is (gyrate)

params.text:
4. WHAT THE THREE PICTURES SAY

COUNT THE ICE: how many molecules still sit in the honeycomb, frame
by frame. It starts well below 768, because a molecule on the
surface has too few neighbours to pass the test. Within half a
picosecond it drops in both runs: once the molecules shiver, some
fail the strict test even though the crystal is still there. After
that, the cold line stays nearly flat and the warm line falls to
zero. That fall is the melting.

SIZE: the radius of gyration, roughly how far the molecules are
from the middle, on average. The warm one shrinks, for two reasons:
a ball is more compact than a cube, and liquid water packs its
molecules closer together than ice does. That is why ice floats,
and why a full bottle of water bursts in a freezer.

THE MOVIE: one dot per molecule, its oxygen. Press play; drag to
turn it. Look straight down the z axis of the cold cube to see the
six-sided channels running through the ice.
